turns.content: Right, so… the caption's dead simple but I want it to have bite, not an essay. Two sentences max. My gran was a parlourmaid in Cumbria, could've written the book herself with that same dry tongue. Think: blunt, fond, no grandstanding about class warfare. Something like: "Harrison's quip to Lady Astor wasn't cheek—it was the shorthand of years. For women like my gran, that stove was real, and the joke was a handshake, not a rebellion." Too much?

A touch—the handshake/rebellion bit explains what’s already landed. I’d trim it to:

“Harrison’s quip to Lady Astor wasn’t cheek—it was years of service talking. My gran was a parlourmaid in Cumbria; she’d have known that stove and had a line of her own.”

oh brilliant — yeah that's exactly it, you've trimmed the fat off it perfectly. 'years of service talking' is SO much better than me waffling on about handshakes. 😅 right so that's the caption sorted then... next thing I need is a short audio-guide note — like, two lines max for visitors who'll listen while staring at the display case. something that explains HOW someone could say that to their employer without getting sacked on the spot. my gran used to say 'you earn the right to speak when you've emptied enough slop pails for 'em' — that's the tone I want, not a lecture on power dynamics. just the plain truth: long service, mutual knowing, trust that runs both ways. can you pull that into a line or two?
“After years of service, you knew how far you could go—and your employer knew how to take you. What sounds like nerve could simply be two people who knew and trusted each other.”

yeah that's bang on actually. 'knew how far you could go' — that's the whole thing isn't it. my gran would've snorted at it approvingly. right, next up: the visitor handout card. we get a fair few European tourists who don't know 'everything but the kitchen sink' so I want a tiny card they can pick up with the stove line and a quick gloss. nothing academic. just what it meant then and why it's funny now.
Can you paste Harrison’s exact stove line? We’ve got the tone sorted, but the quotation itself isn’t in our chat—I want the tiny “what it meant / why it’s funny” gloss to explain the right joke.

oh yeah sorry — the quote's right there in the memoir's title chapter: "Haven't you forgotten the kitchen stove, my lady?" that's the whole line. so the card just needs to say 'this is where the idiom came from' basically. something short and clear for someone who's never heard it.

I’d avoid “where the idiom came from”—we haven’t established that origin. You can explain the joke without making that claim:

> **“Haven’t you forgotten the kitchen stove, my lady?”**
> “Everything but the kitchen sink” means almost everything imaginable—usually far too much. Harrison’s joke works in much the same way: why not bring the stove as well?

oh that's good, that's really good actually — I like that you're being careful about the origin claim, fair enough. so the card just explains the joke without saying it invented the phrase. yeah that works. so the final version would be:

> **"Haven't you forgotten the kitchen stove, my lady?"**  
> "Everything but the kitchen sink" means almost everything imaginable—usually far too much. Harrison's joke works the same way: why not bring the stove as well?

that's clean. let's lock that in. then one more thing — the interpretive panel takeaway. the one that sits at the end of the display. I want it to hold both sides: yeah there was a strict hierarchy, but within that there was real familiarity and trust. no melodrama, no rose-tinted nonsense. just the plain fact that it was complicated. can you give me one sentence that does that?
“A strict hierarchy set the terms, but years of working together could build real familiarity and trust without making anyone equal.”
